Electronic devices are usually built from materials that do not like large deformation.

Semiconductor layers, metallic electrodes, batteries, sensors, and displays may tolerate only small strains before their electrical performance deteriorates or their
components crack.

Yet today we routinely talk about flexible displays, wearable sensors, foldable phones, and even electronics that can be stretched with the human body.

This raises a mechanics question:

> **How can an electronic system undergo very large deformation when many of its functional components cannot?**

One answer is surprisingly familiar to a structural engineer.

**Do not require every component to accommodate the same deformation.**

Instead, design the structure so that deformation occurs where it can be tolerated and is suppressed where it cannot.

This idea became a recurring theme in a collaboration that I began around 2010 with Prof. Jeong Sook Ha in Chemical Engineering at Korea University.

Her group was developing highly deformable electronic devices. My role came from a rather different field: structural mechanics.

Over more than a decade, we worked together on semiconductor devices, sensors, energy-storage devices, and integrated stretchable systems. The electronic functions changed
considerably.

The mechanics problem remained remarkably similar.

---

## Stretchability is not the same as material stretchability

Suppose a device is attached to a substrate subjected to a macroscopic tensile strain

$$
\varepsilon_\mathrm{global}
=
\frac{L-L_0}{L_0}.
$$

If every part of the system follows this deformation uniformly, then a 30% extension of the system would imply approximately 30% strain everywhere.

For many electronic materials, that would be disastrous.

But there is no mechanical requirement that the strain must be uniform.

Compatibility requires the connected system to deform continuously. It does **not** require every material point to experience the same strain.

That distinction changes the design problem completely.

Instead of asking

> How can we make the semiconductor survive 30% strain?

we can ask

> **How can a system extend by 30% while keeping the semiconductor strain below its allowable level?**

That is a structural-mechanics problem.

---

## The first strategy: turn stretching into geometry

One of our early approaches used thin interconnections on a prestrained elastomeric substrate.

When the prestrain was released, the interconnections buckled out of plane.

![Thin interconnections can accommodate large macroscopic deformation through geometric changes rather than large material strain. The important feature is the separation
between deformation of the overall substrate and strain in the active electronic region.](Fig01.png){fig-alt="Stretchable nanowire electronic device on a deformable substrate
showing buckled interconnections"}

The mechanism is familiar from structural mechanics.

A straight member subjected to axial displacement must accommodate that displacement primarily through axial strain before instability occurs.

A curved or buckled member has another possibility: it can change its geometry.

Schematically,

$$
\Delta L_\mathrm{system}
=
\Delta L_\mathrm{material}
+
\Delta L_\mathrm{geometry}.
$$

This is a conceptual decomposition rather than a general finite-deformation identity, but it captures the essential idea.

If geometric reconfiguration accounts for most of the imposed displacement, material strain can remain small.

The same principle appears in springs, bellows, corrugated sheets, cables, and compliant mechanisms.

Stretchable electronics brought it to another length scale.

---

## Large system deformation does not imply large device strain

This distinction between **global deformation** and **local strain** became increasingly important in our work.

In stretchable SWCNT logic devices, for example, the system could accommodate prestrain up to 30%, while classical lamination analysis estimated local strains below
approximately 0.6% in the SWCNT channel and Pd electrode regions.

The electronics therefore did not survive because the semiconductor somehow became capable of sustaining 30% strain.

The architecture prevented that strain from reaching the critical region.

This gives the first general mechanics principle:

> **What matters to a vulnerable component is not the deformation of the whole structure, but the local strain transmitted to that component.**

This statement is equally true for an electronic device and for a large engineering structure.

---

## A more powerful idea: engineer the stiffness distribution

Buckling and serpentine interconnections provide geometric strain relief.

But another possibility is even more directly connected to structural mechanics.

Consider two bonded regions having very different stiffnesses.

One is stiff and contains the functional device.

The other is soft and is allowed to deform.

Under an imposed global displacement, deformation does not distribute uniformly between them.

The compliant region attracts deformation.

This led us to heterogeneous substrates consisting of **stiff islands embedded in or connected by a soft elastomer**.

![The heterogeneous substrate deliberately creates stiff regions for functional devices and soft regions for deformation. The objective is not uniform strain but controlled
strain localization.](Fig02.png){fig-alt="Heterogeneous stretchable substrate with stiff device islands and soft connecting regions"}

The principle can be understood with a simple one-dimensional analogy.

Consider two regions in series:

$$
\Delta
=
\Delta_1+\Delta_2.
$$

For an idealized axial system carrying the same force $F$,

$$
\Delta_i
=
\frac{F L_i}{E_i A_i}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{\Delta_1}{\Delta_2}
=
\frac{L_1/(E_1A_1)}
     {L_2/(E_2A_2)}.
$$

If region 1 is much stiffer than region 2,

$$
E_1A_1 \gg E_2A_2,
$$

most of the displacement occurs in region 2.

The actual stretchable substrate is a multidimensional finite-deformation problem, so this simple series model is not quantitatively equivalent.

But the physical principle is the same:

> **Give the deformation a mechanically preferable place to go.**

---

## Strain isolation is a structural design problem

Finite element analysis made this idea visible.

In one of our stretchable microsupercapacitor systems, stiff islands carried the active devices while a much softer polymer film connected neighboring islands.

Under 40% applied uniaxial strain, the calculated strain was approximately 0.47% on the stiff islands but reached approximately 107% in the soft region between them.

The deformation had not disappeared.

It had been **redistributed**.

![Finite element strain contours reveal the central mechanics of the design. Although the complete system is strongly stretched, deformation is concentrated in the compliant
regions while the device islands remain nearly undeformed.](Fig03.png){fig-alt="Finite element strain distribution of stretchable device showing strain concentration in soft
regions"}

This is perhaps the most important figure in this article.

At first sight, a highly nonuniform strain field might look undesirable.

In conventional structural design we often worry about strain or stress concentrations.

Here the opposite is true.

The concentration is intentional.

The objective is not

$$
\varepsilon(\mathbf{x}) \approx \text{constant}.
$$

Instead, we want

$$
\varepsilon_\mathrm{device}
\ll
\varepsilon_\mathrm{system},
$$

while allowing

$$
\varepsilon_\mathrm{soft}
\gg
\varepsilon_\mathrm{device}.
$$

The strain field itself becomes a design variable.

---

## From strain reduction to strain suppression

The idea was subsequently pushed further.

Instead of simply using relatively stiff polymer islands, stiff PET films could be locally implanted inside a very soft Ecoflex substrate.

The stiffness contrast became enormous.

In the biaxially stretchable microsupercapacitor array, finite element analysis indicated that the maximum strain in the protected device region was below approximately
**0.02%**, even when the substrate was subjected to 70% uniaxial or 50% biaxial strain.

Meanwhile, strain in the surrounding Ecoflex could exceed 250%.

This result sounds paradoxical only if we confuse global strain with local strain.

The system is highly stretchable precisely because the deformation is **extremely nonuniform**.

The electronics are protected because another part of the structure willingly takes the deformation.

---

## The interconnection has a different job

Protecting the device islands creates another mechanics problem.

The islands must still communicate electrically.

If two nearly rigid islands move apart, the electrical interconnection between them must accommodate the relative displacement.

This led to two complementary approaches in our work.

One was geometrically compliant metallic interconnections, including serpentine structures that could deform out of plane.

The other was liquid-metal interconnections embedded inside soft substrates.

A liquid-metal conductor does not have to preserve the geometry of a conventional solid wire while the surrounding substrate deforms.

The functional system therefore becomes mechanically heterogeneous:

- stiff regions protect sensitive devices,
- soft regions accommodate deformation,
- compliant or liquid interconnections maintain electrical continuity.

Stretchability emerges from the **architecture of the system**, not from a single extraordinary material.

---

## The same mechanics survived while the electronics changed

Over the following years, the electronic applications became increasingly sophisticated.

The same mechanics architecture was applied to microsupercapacitors, pressure sensors, gas sensors, body-attached multisensor systems, solar-powered devices, and displays.

For example, an encapsulated microsupercapacitor system used stiff PET platforms in Ecoflex so that, under 30% uniaxial stretching, strain on the MSCs was approximately zero
while the thin Ecoflex regions between them experienced much larger deformation.

Later, stretchable QD-LED arrays used stiff NOA63 islands in a soft Eco-PDMS substrate together with liquid-metal interconnections.

The QD-LED system operated under 50% uniaxial and 30% biaxial stretching.

![The later QD-LED array shows the maturation of the concept: functional display pixels remain on protected islands while the surrounding elastomer and liquid-metal
interconnections accommodate the macroscopic deformation.](Fig04.png){fig-alt="Stretchable QD-LED array under uniaxial and biaxial deformation with FEM strain distributions"}

The electronic device had changed dramatically.

The mechanical principle had not.

---

## Why this is structural mechanics

At first sight, a microsupercapacitor or semiconductor array may seem far removed from civil and structural engineering.

Mechanically, however, the questions are familiar.

Where does deformation occur?

Where should stiffness be placed?

Where should compliance be introduced?

How does geometry transform imposed displacement into local strain?

Where will stress or strain concentrate?

How can a vulnerable component be isolated from global deformation?

These are structural mechanics questions independent of scale.

A bridge may be hundreds of meters long and an electronic device only millimeters or micrometers.

The governing reasoning remains recognizable:

$$
\text{loading}
\rightarrow
\text{deformation field}
\rightarrow
\text{strain}
\rightarrow
\text{stress}
\rightarrow
\text{failure or survival}.
$$

For stretchable electronics, the most important step is often the second one:

$$
\boxed{
\text{global deformation}
\not\Rightarrow
\text{uniform local strain}
}
$$

Once that is understood, the design space becomes much larger.

---

## A structural analogy: seismic isolation

There is a useful analogy with earthquake engineering.

A conventional structure may attempt to resist seismic deformation by making structural members stronger and stiffer.

A base-isolated structure takes a different approach.

It deliberately introduces a region where deformation is allowed to occur.

The objective is not to eliminate displacement.

It is to **control where the displacement occurs** so that vulnerable parts of the structure experience less damaging deformation.

Stretchable electronics follow a conceptually similar strategy.

The analogy is not mathematically identical, but the design philosophy is remarkably close:

> **Protect the functional region by giving deformation somewhere safer to go.**

---

## Mechanics as an enabling technology

This experience also changed my view of what mechanics contributes to multidisciplinary research.

Mechanics is sometimes introduced after a device has already been developed, simply to calculate stress or explain why something failed.

Its more powerful role comes earlier.

Mechanics can determine the architecture.

If a semiconductor can tolerate only a small strain, that does not necessarily impose the stretchability limit of the complete device.

Instead we can ask:

- What stiffness distribution isolates the semiconductor?
- What geometry converts extension into rotation or out-of-plane motion?
- Where should compliant regions be placed?
- How should neighboring rigid islands be connected?
- What local strain results from a prescribed macroscopic deformation?

These questions turn mechanics from an **analysis tool** into a **design tool**.

That was an important part of my contribution to this long collaboration.

---

## What comes next?

The early question was:

> Can we make an electronic system stretch?

Today the more interesting question is:

> **Can we design its deformation field?**

That opens several opportunities for mechanics.

### Optimize the stiffness field

Instead of manually choosing the size and spacing of stiff islands, one could formulate the substrate as an optimization problem.

For example,

$$
\min_{\rho(\mathbf{x})}
\max_{\Omega_\mathrm{device}}
\varepsilon_\mathrm{eq}(\mathbf{x})
$$

subject to constraints on global stretchability, device area, manufacturability, and perhaps electrical connectivity.

The spatial stiffness distribution $\rho(\mathbf{x})$ then becomes part of the design.

Topology optimization and computational mechanics could generate architectures that are difficult to discover by intuition alone.

### Design for multiaxial deformation

Human skin and practical foldable devices rarely experience simple uniaxial tension.

They bend, twist, stretch biaxially, wrinkle, and contact other surfaces.

The mechanics therefore moves naturally toward finite deformation, nonlinear constitutive behavior, contact, and multiaxial loading.

### Design for fatigue, not just maximum strain

A device that survives one 50% stretch is not necessarily a durable device.

Repeated folding and stretching introduce questions of:

- interfacial fatigue,
- delamination,
- crack initiation,
- cyclic damage,
- liquid-metal channel reliability,
- and progressive changes in elastomer properties.

For practical devices, the problem increasingly becomes one of **fracture and fatigue mechanics**.

### Treat interfaces as structural components

As strain in the active device approaches zero, other locations may become critical.

Edges of stiff islands, bonded interfaces, electrical contacts, and transitions between materials can develop strong gradients.

Protecting one component can simply move the mechanical problem somewhere else.

Future designs therefore need to optimize not only the islands and soft substrate, but also their interfaces.

### Couple mechanics with device performance

Ultimately the quantity to minimize may not be mechanical strain itself.

A semiconductor, battery, sensor, or display responds differently to deformation.

The more general problem is

$$
\text{deformation}
\rightarrow
\text{local mechanics}
\rightarrow
\text{change in device physics}
\rightarrow
\text{functional performance}.
$$

The next generation of computational design should couple these levels directly.

---

## From finite element analysis to inverse design

There is another important change ahead.

In much of our earlier work, finite element analysis answered the question:

> If we build this geometry, where will the strain go?

Future computational mechanics can reverse the question:

> **If this is the strain field we want, what geometry should we build?**

That is an inverse problem.

With topology optimization, reduced-order models, surrogate models, and machine learning, it becomes possible to search large families of heterogeneous structures
automatically.

The design target might be something like:

$$
\varepsilon_\mathrm{device}<\varepsilon_\mathrm{allowable}
$$

while maximizing

$$
\varepsilon_\mathrm{global},
$$

subject to electrical, thermal, manufacturing, and durability constraints.

That would turn the original idea of strain isolation into a systematic mechanics-based design framework.

---

## The broader lesson

When we started this collaboration more than a decade ago, foldable and stretchable electronics were still largely research concepts.

Today flexible displays and foldable smartphones are commercial products.

Our research should not be interpreted as a direct technological lineage to those products. The materials, manufacturing processes, and commercial architectures are much
broader than any one research program.

But the mechanics question is the same one we were asking from the beginning:

> How can a system undergo large deformation without imposing damaging strain on its functional components?

The answer that emerged repeatedly from our work is simple.

**Do not make every component follow the global deformation.**

Control the deformation field.

Use geometry to absorb displacement.

Use stiffness contrast to redirect strain.

Use compliant interconnections to connect protected regions.

And use mechanics to determine where deformation should—and should not—occur.

---

## Engineering takeaway

> **A stretchable structure does not require every component to stretch. It requires deformation to occur in the right places.**

That principle applies far beyond electronics.

It is a general principle of structural mechanics.
